claim: The thalamus develops from the diencephalic prosomere 2 (p2).
source: The thalamus is a forebrain structure that develops from the diencephalic prosomere 2 (p2) (Puelles and Rubenstein, 2003; Shi et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Puelles and Rubenstein, 2003; Shi et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2018).

claim: The thalamus is primarily composed of cortically projecting excitatory thalamocortical (TC) neurons.
source: The thalamus is a forebrain structure that develops from the diencephalic prosomere 2 (p2) (Puelles and Rubenstein, 2003; Shi et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2018) and is primarily composed of cortically projecting excitatory thalamocortical (TC) neurons, divided into more than 30 individual nuclei in mammals (Clascá et al., 2012; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Jones, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Clascá et al., 2012; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Jones, 2007).

claim: Thalamocortical neurons are divided into more than 30 individual nuclei in mammals.
source: The thalamus is a forebrain structure that develops from the diencephalic prosomere 2 (p2) (Puelles and Rubenstein, 2003; Shi et al., 2017; Wong et al., 2018) and is primarily composed of cortically projecting excitatory thalamocortical (TC) neurons, divided into more than 30 individual nuclei in mammals (Clascá et al., 2012; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Jones, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Clascá et al., 2012; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Jones, 2007).

claim: The function of the thalamus has been historically described as relay of sensory information to the cortex.
source: The function of the thalamus has been historically described as relay of sensory information to the cortex (Cheong et al., 2013; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Piscopo et al., 2013; Shatz, 1996; Sherman and Guillery, 2002; Van der Loos and Woolsey, 1973; Zeater et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The thalamus is critically involved in cognitive processes allowing for behavioural flexibility.
source: Taking into account the diversity of input and output features of TC circuits (Clascá et al., 2012; Guillery, 1995; Herkenham, 1980; Rubio-Garrido et al., 2009; Sherman, 2016), more recent work has shown that the thalamus is also critically involved in cognitive processes allowing for behavioural flexibility (Bolkan et al., 2017; Groh et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2017; Ling et al., 2015; Rikhye et al., 2018a; Rikhye et al., 2018b; Saalmann and Kastner, 2011; Schmitt et al., 2017; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple recent published studies.

claim: Excitatory neurons in the thalamus do not connect with each other.
source: In contrast to cortical networks, excitatory neurons in the thalamus do not connect with each other (Bickford et al., 2008; Hirsch et al., 2015; Jones, 2007; Rikhye et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bickford et al., 2008; Hirsch et al., 2015; Jones, 2007; Rikhye et al., 2018b).

claim: Local connections and computations within TC circuits are dominated by the resident inhibitory, GABA-releasing neurons (interneurons).
source: Instead, local connections and computations within TC circuits are dominated by the resident inhibitory, GABA-releasing neurons (interneurons) (Hirsch et al., 2015; Montero, 1987; Pasik and Pasik, 1976; Sherman, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Hirsch et al., 2015; Montero, 1987; Pasik and Pasik, 1976; Sherman, 2004).

claim: Interneuron numbers and distribution vary widely across species.
source: Interneuron numbers and distribution vary widely across species, suggesting that they are critically involved in the evolution of TC structure and function (Arcelli et al., 1997; Letinic and Rakic, 2001; Rikhye et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Arcelli et al., 1997; Letinic and Rakic, 2001; Rikhye et al., 2018b).

claim: Interneurons are critically involved in the evolution of TC structure and function.
source: Interneuron numbers and distribution vary widely across species, suggesting that they are critically involved in the evolution of TC structure and function (Arcelli et al., 1997; Letinic and Rakic, 2001; Rikhye et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is presented as a suggestion based on the observation of species variation, supported by citations.

claim: There is a correlation between the proportion of interneurons and the size and connectivity of the excitatory thalamus across all amniotes.
source: In particular, comparative studies across all amniotes (reptiles, birds, and mammals) have described a correlation between the proportion of interneurons and the size and connectivity of the excitatory thalamus (Arcelli et al., 1997; Butler, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to comparative studies (Arcelli et al., 1997; Butler, 2008).

claim: In the reptilian thalamus, interneurons have only been identified in the retinorecipient regions.
source: For example, in the reptilian thalamus, which is mostly devoid of descending projections from the cortex, interneurons have only been identified in the retinorecipient regions (Butler, 2008; Kenigfest et al., 1995; Kenigfest et al., 1998; Pritz and Stritzel, 1994; Rio et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Butler, 2008; Kenigfest et al., 1995; Kenigfest et al., 1998; Pritz and Stritzel, 1994; Rio et al., 1992).

claim: In birds, thalamic interneurons are distributed more widely than in reptiles.
source: In birds, however, where reciprocal connections between the thalamus and the cortex are more abundant, thalamic interneurons are distributed more widely (Butler, 2008; Granda and Crossland, 1989; Veenman and Reiner, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Butler, 2008; Granda and Crossland, 1989; Veenman and Reiner, 1994).

claim: In smaller-brained marsupials, bats and mice, interneurons are largely restricted to the visual thalamus and represent only 6% of the total neuronal population.
source: Similarly among mammals, interneurons are largely restricted to the visual thalamus in smaller-brained marsupials, bats and mice, where they represent only 6% of the total neuronal population (Butler, 2008; Evangelio et al., 2018; Seabrook et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Butler, 2008; Evangelio et al., 2018; Seabrook et al., 2013b).

claim: In primates, interneurons are present across the entire thalamus and their proportion increases to around 30%.
source: In primates, on the other hand, where higher order (HO) nuclei driven by cortical inputs are expanded relative to sensory relay (first order, FO) regions (Armstrong, 1979; Baldwin et al., 2017; Butler, 2008; Halley and Krubitzer, 2019; Stephan et al., 1981), interneurons are present across the entire thalamus and their proportion increases to around 30% (Arcelli et al., 1997; Braak and Bachmann, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Arcelli et al., 1997; Braak and Bachmann, 1985).

claim: In the mouse, interneurons in the FO visual thalamus (LGd) originate in the midbrain from an En1+Gata2+Otx2+Sox14+ lineage.
source: We have previously shown that in the mouse, interneurons in the FO visual thalamus, the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGd), originate in the midbrain from an En1+Gata2+Otx2+Sox14+ lineage (Jager et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Jager et al., 2016).

claim: In humans, the DLX1/2-expressing ganglionic eminences (GE) in the telencephalon are the source of interneurons for some of the larger HO thalamic nuclei – the mediodorsal (MD) nucleus and the pulvinar.
source: On the other hand, earlier work in humans has suggested the DLX1/2-expressing ganglionic eminences (GE) in the telencephalon as the source of interneurons for some of the larger HO thalamic nuclei – the mediodorsal (MD) nucleus and the pulvinar (Letinić and Kostović, 1997; Letinic and Rakic, 2001; Rakić and Sidman, 1969).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Letinić and Kostović, 1997; Letinic and Rakic, 2001; Rakić and Sidman, 1969).

claim: Migration from the GE to the thalamus was not detected in the mouse and macaque brain.
source: At the same time, the latter studies were not able to detect any such migration from the GE in the mouse and macaque brain (Letinic and Rakic, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Letinic and Rakic, 2001).

claim: Cortical inhibitory interneuron classes, generated in the subpallium and defined through expression of regulatory programmes, are common to the amniote lineages.
source: This prediction is supported by findings from the cortex demonstrating that its inhibitory interneuron classes, generated in the subpallium and defined through expression of regulatory programmes (i.e. transcription factors), are common to the amniote lineages (Arendt et al., 2019; Metin et al., 2007; Tasic et al., 2018; Tosches et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Arendt et al., 2019; Metin et al., 2007; Tasic et al., 2018; Tosches et al., 2018).

claim: A conserved subpallial origin was demonstrated for cortical interneurons in the cyclostome hagfish.
source: Moreover, a conserved subpallial origin was demonstrated for cortical interneurons in the cyclostome hagfish, and therefore appears to be an ancestral feature of the vertebrate brain (Sugahara et al., 2017; Sugahara et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Sugahara et al., 2017; Sugahara et al., 2016).

claim: A conserved subpallial origin for cortical interneurons appears to be an ancestral feature of the vertebrate brain.
source: Moreover, a conserved subpallial origin was demonstrated for cortical interneurons in the cyclostome hagfish, and therefore appears to be an ancestral feature of the vertebrate brain (Sugahara et al., 2017; Sugahara et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference from the hagfish data, supported by citations.

claim: All LGd interneurons are defined by expression of the transcription factor gene Sox14.
source: We had previously demonstrated that all LGd interneurons are defined by expression of the transcription factor gene Sox14 and presented the Sox14GFP/+ knockin mouse line (Table 1; Crone et al., 2008) as a useful tool to study these cells (Jager et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Jager et al., 2016).

claim: The Sox14GFP/+ knockin mouse line is a useful tool to study LGd interneurons.
source: We had previously demonstrated that all LGd interneurons are defined by expression of the transcription factor gene Sox14 and presented the Sox14GFP/+ knockin mouse line (Table 1; Crone et al., 2008) as a useful tool to study these cells (Jager et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Jager et al., 2016) and the original description of the mouse line (Crone et al., 2008).

claim: The Allen Brain Atlas and DropViz resources identify a Sox14+ transcriptional cluster corresponding to mouse LGd interneurons.
source: Both the Allen Brain Atlas (2015 Allen Institute for Brain Science. Allen Cell Types Database. Available from: celltypes.brain-map.org) and DropViz resources (available from: dropviz.org; Saunders et al., 2018) identify a Sox14+ transcriptional cluster corresponding to mouse LGd interneurons, confirming our previous findings.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to two public databases (Allen Brain Atlas and DropViz) and citation to Saunders et al., 2018.

claim: Sox14 is expressed upon cell-cycle exit within inhibitory lineages in the diencephalon, midbrain, hindbrain, and spinal cord, but not in the telencephalon.
source: Sox14 is expressed upon cell-cycle exit within inhibitory lineages in the diencephalon, midbrain, hindbrain, and spinal cord, but not in the telencephalon (Achim et al., 2013; Delogu et al., 2012; Guo and Li, 2019; Prekop et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Achim et al., 2013; Delogu et al., 2012; Guo and Li, 2019; Prekop et al., 2018).

claim: Automated counting identified a total of 6588 ± 811 (mean ± SEM) GFP+ cells across TC nuclei of both hemispheres in P21 Sox14GFP/+ mice.
source: Automated counting identified a total of 6588 ± 811 (mean ± SEM) GFP+ cells across TC nuclei of both hemispheres spanning the rostrocaudal and mediolateral extensions of the thalamus (n = 3 Sox14GFP/+ at P21).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from automated counting of GFP+ cells in three P21 Sox14GFP/+ mice.

claim: The distribution of GFP+ cells in Sox14GFP/+ mice is not stochastic but skewed towards sensory TC nuclei.
source: Their distribution was not stochastic but skewed instead towards sensory TC nuclei and within sensory modality by a prevalence in FO nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observed distribution pattern of GFP+ cells in the data.

claim: GFP+ cells are most abundant in the visual FO LGd (1234 ± 82) in P21 Sox14GFP/+ mice.
source: The GFP+ cells are most abundant in the visual FO LGd (1234 ± 82) and HO LP (aka pulvinar; 411 ± 110), followed by sensory-motor ventrobasal (VB) complex [ventral posteromedial (VPM; 250 ± 49), ventral posterolateral (VPL; 105 ± 40), ventral anterior lateral (VAL; 4 ± 3) and ventral medial nucleus (VM; 4 ± 2)] and HO posterior nucleus (PO; 99 ± 12), in turn followed by the auditory FO ventral medial geniculate (MGv; 53 ± 12) and HO dorsal medial geniculate nucleus (MGd; 20 ± 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from automated counting in P21 Sox14GFP/+ mice.

claim: Sparse GFP+ cells were detected in limbic TC nuclei: LD (20 ± 7), PF (25 ± 5), and MD (13 ± 6) nuclei in P21 Sox14GFP/+ mice.
source: Sparse GFP+ cells were also detected in limbic TC nuclei: LD (20 ± 7), parafascicular (PF) (25 ± 5), and MD (13 ± 6) nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from automated counting in P21 Sox14GFP/+ mice.

claim: GFP+ neurons are typically found in the caudal-most part of the LD, nearer the LP border.
source: Notably, GFP+ neurons are typically found in the caudal-most part of the LD, nearer the LP border and nearly all GFP+ neurons were in the caudal half of the MD (see also: Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data from the study and reference to Video 1.

claim: Nearly all GFP+ neurons were in the caudal half of the MD.
source: Notably, GFP+ neurons are typically found in the caudal-most part of the LD, nearer the LP border and nearly all GFP+ neurons were in the caudal half of the MD (see also: Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data from the study and reference to Video 1.

claim: All GFP+ cells in TC nuclei of P14 Sox14GFP/+ mice co-expressed Gad1 (100%, n = 3 brains).
source: In these nuclei all GFP+ cells had a GABAergic profile and co-expressed Gad1 (100%, n = 3 brains).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data from three P14 Sox14GFP/+ brains.

claim: In the LGd, VP, and MGv, GFP+ cells represented virtually all GABAergic cells (≥98%).
source: In the LGd, VP, and MGv (i.e. FO sensory relay nuclei) they also represented virtually all GABAergic cells (≥98%, pie charts in Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 22.1 ± 4.0% of the total GABAergic population in TC regions did not express GFP in P14 Sox14GFP/+ mice.
source: Unexpectedly, however, 22.1 ± 4.0% of the total GABAergic population in TC regions did not express GFP (Figure 2B,C; Figure 5Bii), and these GFP-Gad1+ cells appeared spatially largely non-overlapping with the Sox14+ interneuron class and enriched at more rostral TC territory (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from P14 Sox14GFP/+ mice shown in Figures 2B, 2C, and 5Bii.

claim: GFP-Gad1+ cells appeared spatially largely non-overlapping with the Sox14+ interneuron class and enriched at more rostral TC territory.
source: Unexpectedly, however, 22.1 ± 4.0% of the total GABAergic population in TC regions did not express GFP (Figure 2B,C; Figure 5Bii), and these GFP-Gad1+ cells appeared spatially largely non-overlapping with the Sox14+ interneuron class and enriched at more rostral TC territory (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Gad1+ cells are seen populating rostral TC regions during the first five postnatal days.
source: Gad1+ cells are seen populating these rostral TC regions during the first five postnatal days (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution of GFP-Gad1+ cells is skewed towards the limbic HO MD (29.6 ± 4.5%) and LD (19.4 ± 3.1%).
source: In particular, we observed that the distribution of GFP-Gad1+ cells is skewed towards the limbic HO MD (29.6 ± 4.5%) and LD (19.4 ± 3.1%) and the associative HO LP (13.2 ± 1.2%), and in smaller numbers towards the PO.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative distribution data from P14 Sox14GFP/+ mice.

claim: The cumulative distribution of NNDs was significantly shifted to smaller distances within each of the classes (Gad1+Sox14+ and Gad1+Sox14-) than between them (p<1.4 × 10−30, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, n = 3 brains).
source: Indeed, the cumulative distribution of NNDs was significantly shifted to smaller distances within each of the classes than between them (p<1.4 × 10−30, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, n = 3 brains; Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of nearest neighbor distance data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: K-means clustering of thalamic GABAergic interneurons best fit two spatial clusters.
source: The data best fit two spatial clusters, as assessed from the silhouette score (Figure 3Bii,C; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by machine learning analysis shown in Figures 3Bii and 3C.

claim: One spatial cluster corresponded to the Sox14+ cells (contains 94.9 ± 1.4% of all Sox14+ cells).
source: Consistent with the NND analysis, one cluster corresponded to the Sox14+ cells (contains 94.9 ± 1.4% of all Sox14+ cells), and the other to the Sox14- interneurons (contains 81.0 ± 0.3% of all Sox14- cells; Figure 3B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: The other spatial cluster corresponded to the Sox14- interneurons (contains 81.0 ± 0.3% of all Sox14- cells).
source: Consistent with the NND analysis, one cluster corresponded to the Sox14+ cells (contains 94.9 ± 1.4% of all Sox14+ cells), and the other to the Sox14- interneurons (contains 81.0 ± 0.3% of all Sox14- cells; Figure 3B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: The Sox14- cells are located more rostrally and medially compared to the Sox14+ interneurons.
source: The two thalamic molecular GABAergic groups therefore occupy their own respective spatial clusters, with the Sox14- cells located more rostrally and medially compared to the Sox14+ interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial clustering analysis of the data.

claim: Fluorescent ISH for SOX14 and GAD1 mRNAs revealed the widespread presence of SOX14+GAD1+ bona fide interneurons across all major TC nuclei in the neonatal marmoset.
source: Fluorescent ISH for SOX14 and GAD1 mRNAs revealed the widespread presence of SOX14+GAD1+ bona fide interneurons across all major TC nuclei (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: SOX14+ cells were not present in prethalamic structures (RT, ZI) in the marmoset, but detectable in the pregeniculate/subgeniculate (SubG).
source: Reminiscent of the expression pattern observed in the mouse, SOX14+ cells were not present in prethalamic structures [RT, zona incerta (ZI)], but detectable in the pregeniculate/subgeniculate (SubG), the primate homologue of the mouse IGL (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All TC nuclei tested in the marmoset contained mostly SOX14+GAD1+ cells (90.2 ± 0.9%; mean ± SEM), with the exception of the MD and LD.
source: With the exception of the MD and LD, all TC nuclei tested contained mostly SOX14+GAD1+ cells (90.2 ± 0.9%; mean ± SEM; dotted line in Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the marmoset MD and LD, SOX14-GAD1+ cells account for 28.7 ± 6.7% and 52.3 ± 2.8% (mean ± SEM) of the total GAD1+, respectively.
source: Indeed, in the MD and LD SOX14-GAD1+ cells account for 28.7 ± 6.7% and 52.3 ± 2.8% (mean ± SEM) of the total GAD1+, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the Sox14 KO there is a >90% reduction in the number of interneurons in the LGd.
source: We have previously shown that in the Sox14 KO there is a >90% reduction in the number of interneurons in the LGd (Jager et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Jager et al., 2016).

claim: There is a comparable reduction in the number of GFP+ interneurons overall across the LGd, LP, VP, PO, and MG in the Sox14 KO (90.5 ± 1.5%, p=2.7 × 10−4, two-sample two-tailed t-test, n = 3 brains/genotype).
source: We find a comparable reduction in the number of GFP+ interneurons overall across the LGd, LP, VP, PO, and MG in the Sox14 KO (90.5 ± 1.5%, p=2.7 × 10−4, two-sample two-tailed t-test, n = 3 brains/genotype; Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: There was no significant change in the number of Sox14-Gad1+ cells in the Sox14 KO (p=0.4, two-sample two-tailed t-test).
source: Conversely, there was no significant change in the number of Sox14-Gad1+ cells (p=0.4, two-sample two-tailed t-test; Figure 5A,B) and in their distribution across TC regions (Figure 5A,C; p>0.05, chi-squared test, n = 3 brains/genotype).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: There was no significant change in the distribution of Sox14-Gad1+ cells across TC regions in the Sox14 KO (p>0.05, chi-squared test, n = 3 brains/genotype).
source: Conversely, there was no significant change in the number of Sox14-Gad1+ cells (p=0.4, two-sample two-tailed t-test; Figure 5A,B) and in their distribution across TC regions (Figure 5A,C; p>0.05, chi-squared test, n = 3 brains/genotype).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 5A and 5C.

claim: The two TC interneuron populations may already be segregated during development and represent two distinct GABAergic lineages.
source: These results therefore indicate that the two TC interneuron populations may already be segregated during development and represent two distinct GABAergic lineages.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference from the Sox14 knockout data.

claim: LGd interneurons in the mouse derive from the midbrain.
source: LGd interneurons in the mouse derive from the midbrain (Jager et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Jager et al., 2016).

claim: En1+ cells were observed beyond the LGd – in the LP, VP, PO, and MG, where they were also positive for GABA.
source: However, like the Sox14+Gad1+ neurons, En1+ cells were observed beyond the LGd – in the LP, VP, PO, and MG, where they were also positive for GABA (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The distribution of En1+ cells is equivalent to the distribution of Sox14+ INs (p>0.05, chi-squared test).
source: Plotting their distribution confirmed that it is equivalent to the distribution of Sox14+ INs (p>0.05, chi-squared test; Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of distribution data shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: The Sox14+ thalamic interneurons across FO and HO TC nuclei all derive from the midbrain.
source: We therefore conclude that the Sox14+ thalamic interneurons across FO and HO TC nuclei all derive from the midbrain, and simultaneously that the Sox14- GABAergic cells do not; the two classes thus represent distinct inhibitory lineages in TC regions, further supporting their definition as two distinct thalamic interneuron classes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the En1 fate mapping data presented in the study.

claim: The Sox14- GABAergic cells do not derive from the midbrain.
source: We therefore conclude that the Sox14+ thalamic interneurons across FO and HO TC nuclei all derive from the midbrain, and simultaneously that the Sox14- GABAergic cells do not; the two classes thus represent distinct inhibitory lineages in TC regions, further supporting their definition as two distinct thalamic interneuron classes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the En1 fate mapping data presented in the study.

claim: LGd interneurons were found to populate this nucleus in the first postnatal week.
source: Previously, LGd interneurons were found to populate this nucleus in the first postnatal week (Golding et al., 2014; Jager et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Golding et al., 2014; Jager et al., 2016).

claim: At E16.5 no GFP+ cells were present in the thalamus of En1Cre;Rosa26lsl-GFP mice.
source: At E16.5 no GFP+ cells were present in the thalamus.
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data from En1Cre;Rosa26lsl-GFP mice.

claim: From E17.5 to P2.5 the numbers of GFP+ cells progressively increased in all of the regions analysed (LGd, LP, and VP).
source: From E17.5 to P2.5 their numbers progressively increased in all of the regions analysed (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Midbrain-derived interneurons populate the different TC regions following a similar timeline.
source: Midbrain-derived interneurons therefore populate the different TC regions following a similar timeline.
evidence: The claim is supported by the developmental time course data presented in the study.

claim: Midbrain-derived interneurons appear in two ventrally located nuclei (LGd and VP) simultaneously.
source: Interestingly, they appear in two ventrally located nuclei (i.e. LGd and VP) simultaneously (Figure 7A,B), implying they use distinct routes to reach them.
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Midbrain-derived interneurons use distinct routes to reach the LGd and VP.
source: Interestingly, they appear in two ventrally located nuclei (i.e. LGd and VP) simultaneously (Figure 7A,B), implying they use distinct routes to reach them.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference from the simultaneous appearance in two nuclei.

claim: GFP+ cells migrate into the LGd, LP, and VP in a caudo-rostral and dorso-ventral direction at a population level.
source: Heat maps indicate that at a population level (integrated across dimensions), GFP+ cells migrate into the LGd, LP, and VP in a caudo-rostral and dorso-ventral direction (Figure 7D), consistent with the position of the thalamus in the brain relative to their midbrain origin.
evidence: The claim is supported by leading process orientation analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: GFP+ precursors in the LGd and LP have a dominant medio-lateral orientation.
source: However, GFP+ precursors in the LGd and LP have a dominant medio-lateral orientation, while those in the VP an opposite, latero-medial orientation, as can also be seen from polar histograms (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by leading process orientation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GFP+ precursors in the VP have a dominant latero-medial orientation.
source: However, GFP+ precursors in the LGd and LP have a dominant medio-lateral orientation, while those in the VP an opposite, latero-medial orientation, as can also be seen from polar histograms (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by leading process orientation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Midbrain-derived interneuron precursors enter TC regions simultaneously in two distinct streams, one migrating rostro-ventro-laterally to the LGd and LP, and the other rostro-ventro-medially to the VP.
source: This suggests that midbrain-derived interneuron precursors enter TC regions simultaneously in two distinct streams, one migrating rostro-ventro-laterally to the LGd and LP, and the other rostro-ventro-medially to the VP, indicating a split between visual (LGd, LP) and somatosensory (VP) TC nuclei.
evidence: The claim is presented as an inference from the leading process orientation data.

claim: Within inhibitory clusters from the diencephalon, Sox14 and Pvalb show largely non-overlapping expression.
source: We made use of DropViz data [available from: dropviz.org; (Saunders et al., 2018)] and observed that within inhibitory clusters from the diencephalon, Sox14 and Pvalb show largely non-overlapping expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of DropViz data (Saunders et al., 2018).

claim: Pvalb is expressed by the prethalamic RT.
source: It is known that Pvalb is expressed by the prethalamic RT (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017) and by telencephalic interneuron subtypes derived from the GE (Marín and Rubenstein, 2001; Tasic et al., 2016; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).

claim: Pvalb is expressed by telencephalic interneuron subtypes derived from the GE.
source: It is known that Pvalb is expressed by the prethalamic RT (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017) and by telencephalic interneuron subtypes derived from the GE (Marín and Rubenstein, 2001; Tasic et al., 2016; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Marín and Rubenstein, 2001; Tasic et al., 2016; Tremblay et al., 2016).

claim: At P14, GFP was detected at the nuclear membrane of GABA-expressing neurons within the same regions populated by the Sox14- interneurons in PvalbCre;Rosa26lsl-nuclearGFP mice.

claim: The telencephalic GE are an unlikely source of thalamic interneurons in the mouse.
source: Importantly, Lhx6 marks also the vast majority of GE-derived telencephalic interneurons (Zhao et al., 2008), hence this result further confirms that the telencephalic GE are an unlikely source of thalamic interneurons in the mouse.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion from the Lhx6 fate mapping data and citation to Zhao et al., 2008.

claim: The rarer Sox14- thalamic interneuron class originates from Dlx5+Foxd1+ progenitors in the prethalamus.
source: Altogether, we therefore conclude that the rarer Sox14- thalamic interneuron class is a distinct lineage compared to the larger, midbrain-born Sox14+ thalamic interneuron class, and that originates from Dlx5+Foxd1+ progenitors in the prethalamus.
evidence: The claim is presented as a conclusion from the fate mapping experiments.

claim: The study reveals a previously unappreciated complexity of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse TC nuclei.
source: Our study reveals a previously unappreciated complexity of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse TC nuclei, demonstrating that interneurons are not restricted to the FO visual thalamus, but present across modalities and hierarchical levels, including limbic structures.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Interneurons are not restricted to the FO visual thalamus, but present across modalities and hierarchical levels, including limbic structures.

evidence: The claim is a summary statement of the study's findings from fate mapping experiments.

claim: The two ontogenetic programmes contribute differentially to interneuron numbers, with the midbrain-derived class overwhelmingly more abundant.

claim: The midbrain-derived interneurons depend on the Sox14 transcription factor.
source: The midbrain-derived interneurons depend on the Sox14 transcription factor, a gene that we had previously implicated in LGd interneuron differentiation (Jager et al., 2016) and a known postmitotic marker for GABAergic subtype neurogenesis in the brainstem (Achim et al., 2013; Achim et al., 2014; Huisman et al., 2019; Prekop et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by the Sox14 knockout data and citations to published studies.

claim: Sox14 is a known postmitotic marker for GABAergic subtype neurogenesis in the brainstem.
source: The midbrain-derived interneurons depend on the Sox14 transcription factor, a gene that we had previously implicated in LGd interneuron differentiation (Jager et al., 2016) and a known postmitotic marker for GABAergic subtype neurogenesis in the brainstem (Achim et al., 2013; Achim et al., 2014; Huisman et al., 2019; Prekop et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Achim et al., 2013; Achim et al., 2014; Huisman et al., 2019; Prekop et al., 2018).

claim: The midbrain ontogenetic programme may be the dominant source of thalamic interneurons in larger-brained mammals.
source: Rather than representing a peculiarity of mice, the midbrain ontogenetic programme may be the dominant source of thalamic interneurons in larger-brained mammals, as suggested by the identification of SOX14+GAD1+ interneurons across virtually all TC nuclei in the interneuron-rich thalamus of the marmoset.
evidence: The claim is presented as a speculation based on the marmoset data.

claim: SOX14 expression differentiates between interneuron subclasses in the macaque and human thalamus.
source: This finding is consistent with the recent report of molecularly defined classes of GABAergic interneurons in the macaque and human thalamus, where SOX14 expression differentiates between interneuron subclasses. Interestingly, SOX14- interneurons are DLX1-6+, in agreement with the ontogenetic plan that we propose here (Bakken et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent published study (Bakken et al., 2020).

claim: SOX14- interneurons in the macaque and human thalamus are DLX1-6+.
source: This finding is consistent with the recent report of molecularly defined classes of GABAergic interneurons in the macaque and human thalamus, where SOX14 expression differentiates between interneuron subclasses. Interestingly, SOX14- interneurons are DLX1-6+, in agreement with the ontogenetic plan that we propose here (Bakken et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent published study (Bakken et al., 2020).

claim: Jones previously described late appearance of interneurons in the ferret and macaque thalamus, progressively from caudal towards rostral nuclei.
source: Consistent with a conserved midbrain ontogeny of thalamic interneurons, Jones previously described late appearance of interneurons in the ferret and macaque thalamus, progressively from caudal towards rostral nuclei (Hayes et al., 2003; Jones, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Hayes et al., 2003; Jones, 2002).

claim: Both GAD1 and SOX14 expression increase in the dorsal thalamus in the mid-prenatal period (from postconception week 16) in humans.
source: It can also be seen from the BrainSpan Atlas of the Developing Human Brain [BrainSpan Atlas of the Developing Human Brain; available from: http://www.brainspan.org; (Miller et al., 2014)] that both GAD1 and SOX14 expression increase in the dorsal thalamus in the mid-prenatal period (from postconception week 16), which is also consistent with a migration of midbrain-born interneurons into these regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the BrainSpan Atlas (Miller et al., 2014).

claim: Grafting experiments using chick and quail embryos demonstrated a potential for midbrain cells to populate retino-recipient nuclei in the chick diencephalon.
source: Interestingly, grafting experiments using chick and quail embryos demonstrated a potential for midbrain cells to populate retino-recipient nuclei in the chick diencephalon (Martinez and Alvarado-Mallart, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Martinez and Alvarado-Mallart, 1989).

claim: Lineage tracing in chick, using a retroviral library, indicated that clonally related siblings can populate both the diencephalon and mesencephalon.
source: Relatedly, lineage tracing in chick, using a retroviral library, indicated that clonally related siblings can populate both the diencephalon and mesencephalon (Golden and Cepko, 1996), in keeping with a revised model of evolutionary relationship of caudal diencephalon and midbrain (Albuixech-Crespo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Golden and Cepko, 1996; Albuixech-Crespo et al., 2017).

claim: The distribution of Sox14+ interneurons observed in the mouse is similar to the one described in the opossum.
source: The distribution of Sox14+ interneurons observed in the mouse is similar to the one described in the opossum, a living marsupial thought to resemble early mammals in the fossil record (Penny et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Penny et al., 1984).

claim: Interneurons occupy the lateral subdivision of the LP in the adult opossum thalamus.
source: Intriguingly, rather than spreading throughout the nucleus, interneurons occupy the lateral subdivision of the LP in the adult opossum thalamus (Penny et al., 1984), reminiscent of the route taken by migrating midbrain-derived interneuron precursors in the developing mouse thalamus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Penny et al., 1984).

claim: In both the mouse and marmoset, Sox14-Gad1+ interneurons have drastically more restricted distribution.
source: While the emerging picture points to a midbrain ontogeny for the largest fraction of thalamic interneurons, this is not sufficient to explain the overall developmental complexity of interneurons in the thalamus. In both the mouse and marmoset, we now report the presence of Sox14-Gad1+ interneurons with drastically more restricted distribution.
evidence: The claim is supported by the distribution data presented in the study.

source: The forebrain-derived interneurons are not found in precisely the same set of associative TC nuclei across mouse and marmoset, while the forebrain-derived human lineage previously described is thought to be an evolutionary innovation that migrates into the thalamus from the GE along transient anatomical structures that are not present in rodents and non-human primates (Letinić and Kostović, 1997).
